CHIEF COMPLAINT
Annual exam.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Ralph is a 62-year-old male with a past medical history of depression, prior lobectomy, and hypertension, who presents for his annual exam. He reports feeling relatively well, though he had a stressful spring with allergies/pollen and moving his oldest daughter into her college dorm. His depression is well-managed on Prozac, and he stays on top of his medications. Regarding his hypertension, he takes Norvasc regularly during the business week, though he occasionally forgets it on the weekends when he is on the go. He reports some nasal congestion due to pollen and heat. He runs 4 to 5 miles daily and notes occasional shortness of breath and chest pounding during runs in hot/humid weather, though it usually resolves. 

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Endorses nasal congestion from pollen and occasional shortness of breath/chest pounding with exertion (running in the heat/humidity). Otherwise, review of systems is negative for cough or muscle aches (as noted on the review of systems sheet).

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
- Vital signs: Blood pressure 120/80 mmHg in the office today.
- Heart: 2/6 systolic ejection murmur.
- Lungs: Clear to auscultation; no lower extremity edema.
- Sinuses: Pain to palpation of the sinuses, indicating congestion.

RESULTS
- EKG: Completely normal.
- Chest X-ray: Normal, showing no issues related to the prior lobectomy.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Depression: Doing very well on current strategy. Continue Prozac 20 mg daily. Refill ordered.
2. Prior Lobectomy / Pulmonary: No further workup or follow-up with the surgeon is needed. Breathing function is fine with heavy exercise.
3. Hypertension: Controlled. Continue current medication (Norvasc). Encourage consistency with weekend dosing.
4. Cardiac murmur: 2/6 systolic ejection murmur noted on exam. Ordered an echocardiogram to evaluate further; will follow up with results.
5. Routine Care: Routine blood work ordered. Follow-up will be conducted via the patient portal.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Fatigue, lightheadedness, and feeling out of sorts for about 5 weeks.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
The patient is a 58-year-old male with a past medical history of congestive heart failure and hypertension who presents for follow-up of his chronic problems. He reports feeling "out of sorts," tired, fatigued, and experiencing occasional lightheadedness starting around Labor Day (about 5 weeks ago). He notes occasional bloating, shortness of breath when exerting energy on home projects, slight chest cramps that go away after about an hour, and a slight cough. He admits to eating out a lot and having a less optimal diet recently due to kitchen renovations starting over Labor Day weekend. He denies fevers, chills, nausea, vomiting, or diarrhea. He reports taking his medications and monitoring his blood pressure regularly at home with a cuff.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Positive for fatigue, lightheadedness, occasional bloating, shortness of breath with exertion, slight chest cramps, and a slight cough. Negative for fevers, chills, nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Vital signs: Blood pressure, heart rate, and oxygenation look good in the office.
Neck: Jugular venous distention to about 8 centimeters.
Heart: 3/6 systolic ejection murmur, previously noted.
Lungs: Fine crackles at the bases bilaterally.
Extremities: 1+ pitting edema in the lower extremities.

RESULTS
Chest X-ray: Shows a little bit of fluid in the lungs, attributed to heart failure.
Echocardiogram (from about 4 months ago): Shows reduced pumping function of the heart at 45% and mitral regurgitation (leaky valve).

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Congestive heart failure: Patient is retaining fluid. 
   - Increase Lasix to 80 mg once a day.
   - Weigh daily and call if gaining weight or experiencing shortness of breath.
   - Order a repeat echocardiogram.
2. Hypertension: Managed well at this time.
   - Continue Lisinopril 20 mg a day.
   - Continue recording blood pressures at home and report via patient portal if elevated.

Right finger pain.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Sharon Brooks is a 48-year-old female presenting with right finger pain. The patient reports that on Sunday (about four days ago), while skiing and going over moguls, her ski strap got caught on her finger and bent it back. She tried applying ice and taking ibuprofen, but it is still very painful. Movement makes the pain worse. 

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Not discussed.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Tenderness is present over the distal phalanx (tip of the finger) and over the joint itself. No tenderness over the proximal joint or the metacarpophalangeal joint (above the knuckle). Pain with flexion. Patient is able to bend the finger, extend it, and touch her thumb with it.

RESULTS
X-rays of the right finger look normal with no fractures; everything lines up pretty well.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
- Diagnosis: Right hand index finger contusion on the tip of the finger.
- Treatment: Aluminum foam splint.
- Medication: Motrin 600 mg every 6 hours for about a week.
- Follow-up: Call and return if it does not get better.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Iron deficiency anemia.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Christina Cooper is a 65-year-old female referred by Dr. Diane Nelson for long-standing iron deficiency anemia, dating back to when she was 13 years old. The patient recently tried to donate blood in December and was told she was anemic. She reports feeling fatigued during the day, feverish with chills at times, shortness of breath and wheezing with activity, and headaches. She also notes chilling sensations, easily getting cold, and worsening anxiety and depression. She had heavy periods in the past until a hysterectomy in 1996. Her last colonoscopy was about 5 to 6 years ago and was reported as normal. She recently restarted taking ferrous sulfate 25 mg tablets twice daily and over-the-counter vitamin B12.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
General: Positive for fatigue, feverish feeling, and chills.
Head: Positive for headaches.
Respiratory: Positive for shortness of breath and wheezing with activity.
Gastrointestinal: No reported acute issues; remote history of heavy periods prior to 1996 hysterectomy.
Psychiatric: Positive for worsening anxiety and depression.
All other systems reviewed and negative.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
General: Pleasant 65-year-old female.
Heart: Normal heart exam.
Lungs: Normal lung exam.
Abdomen: Soft, non-tender, with no tenderness to palpation.
Overall physical exam is normal without significant findings.

RESULTS
Not discussed.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Iron deficiency anemia:
   - Continue ferrous sulfate 25 mg by mouth twice daily, to be taken with orange juice (vitamin C) to improve iron absorption, for 8-12 weeks, then reassess blood work (CBC, iron, ferritin, B12, and folate).
   - Schedule an upper endoscopy (EGD) and colonoscopy to assess for potential sources of anemia or GI bleed.
   - If EGD and colonoscopy are inconclusive, consider a capsule endoscopy.
2. Hematology referral:
   - Send a referral to Dr. Flores (hematologist) for evaluation regarding potential IV iron or other management.
3. Patient instructions:
   - Stop by on the way out to schedule the EGD, colonoscopy, and hematology appointment with Dr. flores.
   - Review instructions for the bowel prep.
   - Call the clinic with any questions or worsening symptoms.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Chest pain, fall, and shortness of breath following an emergency department visit.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
The patient is a male who presents following a recent emergency department visit after experiencing a fall while walking outside. He reports having chest pain prior to the fall, which he initially attributed to a pulled muscle or heartburn, and noted some shortness of breath that he tried to walk off. He admits to missing doses of his blood pressure medications every now and then, taking only one today; his BP in the ER was 200/90. He admits to poor dietary habits, including eating salty foods like chips, especially around the holidays. He currently feels a little out of breath, denies sleep problems, and reports slight chest pain here and there that he thought was heartburn. He has not yet purchased a home blood pressure cuff. He reports smoking about once every week.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
General: Out of breath, otherwise feels okay. Denies sleep problems (sleeps like a rock).
Cardiovascular: Reports chest pain (thought to be heartburn) and past shortness of breath.
Respiratory: Shortness of breath with exertion. Lungs clear.
All other systems not discussed.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Vital Signs: Blood pressure in the office today is 128/72. Other vital signs look good.
Neck: No jugular venous distention.
Heart: 2/6 systolic ejection murmur, heard previously and stable.
Lungs: Clear bilaterally.
Extremities: Lower extremities show trace edema.

RESULTS
Echocardiogram (from ER visit): Preserved ejection fraction of 55%, normal diastolic filling, and mild to moderate mitral regurgitation.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Congestive heart failure (CHF) exacerbation, likely caused by dietary indiscretion and uncontrolled hypertension.
   - Continue Bumex 2 mg once daily; take medications consistently.
   - Weigh daily (get a scale at home); call if weight increases by 3 pounds in 2 days.
   - Consult nutrition for dietary advice, specifically watching salty foods.
2. Hypertension.
   - Continue Cozaar 100 mg daily.
   - Continue Norvasc 5 mg once daily.
   - Obtain a home blood pressure cuff to track blood pressure.
3. Order renal artery ultrasound to rule out secondary causes.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Sharp pain on the right side of the abdomen below the ribs.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Russell is a male presenting with sharp pain on the right side of his abdomen below the ribs for the last several days. The pain radiates to the lower abdomen and into the groin. It comes and goes, is pretty bad when present, and he feels like he cannot find a comfortable position. He reports burning with urination and urine that looks a little dark sometimes, but no frank blood. He has taken Tylenol without much relief. He feels nauseated but has not vomited. He has a history of previous kidney stones that he was able to pass, and a family history of kidney stones (father).

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Not discussed.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Abdomen: No tenderness to palpation, no evidence of rebound or guarding, no peritoneal signs.
Back/Flank: Positive CVA tenderness on the right flank.

RESULTS
CT scan of the abdomen ordered by primary care doctor shows a 0.5 cm kidney stone located in the proximal right ureter, with no evidence of hydronephrosis.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Acute nephrolithiasis (kidney stone):
- Recommend pushing fluids to facilitate urination and help pass the stone.
- Prescribed oxycodone 5 mg every 6 to 8 hours as needed for pain; can continue to alternate with Tylenol.
- Provide a urine strainer to catch the stone for testing when passed.
- Order a basic metabolic panel, urinalysis, and urine culture.
- Follow-up in 1 to 2 weeks. Discussed further treatment options if symptoms persist, including lithotripsy or ureteroscopy.
- Instructed to contact the clinic if symptoms worsen.

Left shoulder pain.

Wayne is a very active male presenting with left shoulder pain for approximately three weeks. He does not recall a specific acute injury, but notes he has been doing a lot of work renovating his basement and suspects it may be related. Negative for numbness or tingling in the arms or hands. Otherwise, not discussed.

Neurovascular (Left Arm): Capillary refill is less than 3 seconds. Sensation is intact to light touch.

RESULTS
Shoulder X-ray: Reviewed, shows no fractures.

- Continue taking Tylenol as needed.
- Discussed potential for a steroid injection if symptoms do not improve.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Worsening headaches and a newly diagnosed pituitary lesion.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
The patient is a 52-year-old male with a newly diagnosed pituitary lesion, seen in consultation at the request of Dr. Henry Howard for possible surgical intervention. Mr. Ward presented to Dr. Howard on 3/1/21 complaining of worsening headaches over the past few months, with no prior history of headaches. Workup initiated by Dr. Howard included a brain MRI and serology, which incidentally discovered a pituitary lesion. 

The patient reports the headaches have been going on for about three months, located behind his eyes, described as a dull nagging ache. The onset was gradual, starting at a 3/10 severity and worsening over time to a 6/10 severity. Headaches tend to be worse in the morning, last a few hours at a time, and nothing makes them better or worse. Tylenol was tried a few times without relief and was stopped. He denies feeling sick, fever, rashes, neck stiffness, numbness, tingling, or passing out. He notes that recently he seems to be bumping into door frames. He denies changes in his vision or balance.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Constitutional: Denies fever, feeling sick.
Eyes: Denies vision changes (notes eyes checked in fall, though visual field testing reveals bitemporal hemianopia and bumping into door frames).
Neurological: Denies headaches (other than chief complaint), numbness, tingling, weakness, passing out.
All other systems reviewed and negative unless mentioned above.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
General: Alert, oriented to time, place, and person. Affect is appropriate, speech is fluent.
Cranial Nerves: Grossly intact. Visual acuity and eye movements are normal. Pupils are equal and reactive. Color vision is normal. Visual field testing reveals bitemporal hemianopia.
Extremities: No focal, motor, or sensory deficit in the upper or lower extremities.

RESULTS
Labs (dated 3/3/21): CBC, unates, coagulation, and CRP were all normal. Pituitary hormone profile demonstrates a low TSH; all other results were normal.
Radiology (MRI brain with contrast from 3/4/21): Reveals a pituitary lesion with elevation and compression of the optic chiasm. Ventricles are normal in size, and no other abnormalities are noted.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Pituitary adenoma (benign-appearing, incidentally discovered during workup for worsening headaches). 
2. Symptomatic with clinical and radiographical evidence of optic chiasmal compression. Surgical intervention to excise and decompress the pituitary fossa is indicated.
3. Recommended transsphenoidal approach for surgery (minimally invasive through the sphenoid sinus). Discussed risks of anesthesia and surgery, including heart attack, stroke, death, infection, need for further surgery, wound issues, CSF leak, prolonged hospitalization, seizure, permanent numbness, weakness, and difficulty speaking.
4. Referral to ophthalmology for a full exam and formal visual field test to map peripheral vision prior to surgery and monitor post-surgery.
5. Patient to meet with the surgery scheduler, Deborah, on the way out to schedule the procedure promptly and arrange the pre-surgery visual field test.

Recently, he noticed a foul smell, yellow drainage, and soft mushy skin under the unroofed blister. His primary care doctor started him on antibiotics 6 days ago (10-day course prescribed). He reports a temperature of 99.7 F checked by his wife, chills requiring an extra blanket, and more recently, the wound has turned black around the outside, with calf cramping, a red streak coming up the front of his ankle along the inside of his calf, and the area is very hot. He notes throbbing pain like a fire poker in the bottom of his foot, calf hardness, and pain radiating to his knee behind the kneecap when pushed. He also reports coughing a lot for the last two days and difficulty catching his breath when walking around the house. Blood sugars have been trending in the 300s to 400s over the last two weeks with one spike to 500-600, whereas his baseline A1c has been stable at 6.7%. He recently went on a hike to Charlie's Bunion about 3 or 4 days after getting a new pair of diabetic shoes and inserts.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Constitutional: Positive for subjective fever (99.7 F), chills, and a cough. Negative for nausea or vomiting.
Respiratory: Positive for difficulty catching breath when walking around the house.
Cardiovascular: Not discussed.
Gastrointestinal: Not discussed.
Genitourinary: Not discussed.
Musculoskeletal: Positive for right calf cramping, hard calf muscle, and pain radiating to the knee.
Skin: Positive for right heel blister, foul odor, yellow drainage, black necrotic tissue, and a red streak on the inner calf.

Hematologic/Lymphatic: Not discussed.
Allergic/Immunologic: Not discussed.

Vital Signs: Slight fever noted; overall vitals look good.

RESULTS
Right foot X-ray: No evidence of osteomyelitis (no infection of the bone).

1. Non-healing diabetic right foot ulcer with necrosis, cellulitis, and possible ascending lymphangitis / deep space infection.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Richard is a patient who presents with a tick bite located around his right knee, which occurred over a week ago. He reports that the area burns, feels warm, and is annoying, though he wonders if it might be a spider bite. He reports a general feeling of not doing well and a headache since the tick bite, but denies fever, chills, joint pain other than his typical arthritic pain, shortness of breath, dizziness, cough, or difficulty moving his knee/walking. He recently went hunting a couple of weeks ago and spends time outdoors in the woods and yard. He has no prior history of tick bites or Lyme disease.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
General: Denies fever or chills; reports a general feeling of not doing well and a headache since the tick bite.
Respiratory: Denies cough or shortness of breath.
Cardiovascular: Denies dizziness.
Musculoskeletal: Denies joint pain in elbows or shoulders (reports only typical arthritic pain); denies difficulty moving the knee or problems walking.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Vitals: Blood pressure 122/70, heart rate 67, temperature 98.4 F.
Heart: Regular rate and rhythm; no murmur, rub, or gallop.
Lungs: Clear to auscultation bilaterally.
Right Knee: Erythema, edema, and an area of fluctuance over the right patella. Pain to palpation of the right anterior knee. Full range of motion of the right knee with no pain on bending, just typical grinding.
Skin: Bull's-eye rash over the right knee.

RESULTS
Not discussed.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Tick bite / suspected Lyme disease: Concerned for Lyme disease based on the presentation of the right knee and bull's-eye rash. 
- Start doxycycline 100 mg twice a day for about 3 weeks.
- Send Lyme titer and Western blot.
2. Hypertension: Doing well on current regimen. 
- Continue lisinopril 20 mg once a day.
- Order a lipid panel to check cholesterol.
3. Diabetes Mellitus: Blood sugars running in the 120s. 
- Continue metformin 1,000 mg twice a day.
- Order a hemoglobin A1c.
4. Renal function: 
- Order a basic metabolic panel to ensure kidney function is stable given the metformin use.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Left knee pain.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
The patient is a female presenting with occasional left knee pain and instability. The left knee gives out occasionally, less than once a day when walking, lasting a very short time and passing as quickly as it comes. She feels like she is going to fall but usually catches herself, and holding a grocery cart helps. She denies any popping sounds, specific injuries, falls, or trauma to the knee. She has not taken any pain medication as the pain does not last long. The issue is not significantly interfering with her daily activities, though she has a trip planned to Columbus, Georgia, in the next month for a Lion's Club function where she anticipates a lot of walking, and she is choosing not to participate in line dancing to avoid the risk of her knee giving out.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Blood pressure: Patient reports home blood pressures are running around 120/70. 
Diabetes mellitus: Patient reports morning fasting blood sugars have been running a little higher at about 130. 
All other systems not discussed.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Vital Signs: Temperature 98.2, pulse 72, respirations 16, blood pressure 122/70.
General: No acute distress.
Cardiovascular: Nice regular rate and rhythm; faint 2/6 systolic ejection murmur at the left base.
Respiratory: Lungs clear to auscultation bilaterally.
Left Knee Examination: No ecchymosis or edema, no effusion, no pain to palpation of the left medial knee. No decreased range of motion. Negative varus and valgus tests. 

RESULTS
Left knee x-ray reviewed: showed no evidence of fracture or bony abnormality.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Left knee pain: Suspect arthritis. Prescribe meloxicam 15 mg daily. Consider physical therapy to strengthen muscles around the area and prevent further problems.
2. Hypertension: Continue lisinopril at 20 mg a day. Order an echocardiogram to evaluate the heart murmur.
3. Diabetes mellitus: Order a hemoglobin A1c to evaluate if metformin adjustments are needed. Order a lipid panel.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Right knee pain and hypertension follow-up.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Patient is a philip presenting with right knee pain that occurred one week ago while doing work on his property, where he slipped and fell down. He felt something pop and notes the knee is a little bit swollen. Pain is rated 4-5 out of 10 with mobility, and minimal to none when stationary. Pain is aggravated by flexing, moving up and down, and putting pressure on the knee. He has been taking ibuprofen for swelling. 
For hypertension, he takes lisinopril 20 mg daily and reports taking it regularly. Blood pressure today in the office was 150/70. Patient acknowledges his diet has gotten out of control since the pandemic and he has not made changes regarding reducing sodium intake.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
General: Not discussed.
Constitutional: Not discussed.
Eyes: Not discussed.
Ears, Nose, Throat: Not discussed.
Cardiovascular: Denies chest pain.
Respiratory: Denies shortness of breath.
Gastrointestinal: Denies belly pain.
Genitourinary: Not discussed.
Musculoskeletal: Positive for right knee pain, popping sensation, swelling, and pain with flexion/extension. Denies pain on the outside of the knee.
Skin: Not discussed.
Neurological: Not discussed.
Psychiatric: Not discussed.
Endocrine: Not discussed.
Hematologic/Lymphatic: Not discussed.
Allergic/Immunologic: Not discussed.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Vitals: Blood pressure 150/70.
Lungs: Clear bilaterally; no wheezes or crackles.
Heart: Grade 2/6 systolic ejection murmur.
Right Knee Exam: Pain to palpation of the medial aspect of the right knee. Pain with flexion and extension. Edema around the knee and effusion (fluid) present. No pain upon palpation of the outside of the knee.

RESULTS
Right knee X-ray: No fractures or bony abnormalities.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Right medial collateral ligament (MCL) strain: Result of a fall/twist while working.
   - Prescribe ibuprofen 800 mg twice a day for pain and swelling.
   - Place patient in a knee brace to support muscles and allow healing.
   - Ice the knee for 20 minutes at a time, 3 to 4 times a day.
   - Elevate the leg and stay off the leg for a couple of weeks.
2. Hypertension: Blood pressure 150/70 today, likely white coat syndrome.
   - Continue lisinopril 20 mg daily.
   - Referral to nutrition to help with diet and reducing sodium intake, with the ultimate goal of lowering blood pressure and potentially discontinuing medication.
